content:
When arthritis and frailty make walking distances difficult, a mobility scooter can help you keep doing shopping, visits and outings.

This guide covers things to consider before getting a scooter. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Could a scooter help?

  • You can walk short distances but not as far as you need to.
  • Fatigue or pain stops you going out.
  • You want to stay independent for local trips.

The rules

Class 2 scooters can be used on pavements with a top speed of 4mph. Class 3 scooters can be used on roads with a top speed of 8mph, and must be registered with the DVLA. You do not need a licence, but you should be able to see well enough and control the scooter safely. Insurance is recommended.

Choosing a scooter

  • Try different models at a mobility centre or shop.
  • Check the seat, controls and getting on and off with your joints.
  • Consider tiller controls if hands are painful.
  • Check where you will store and charge it.
  • Think about whether it needs to fit in a car.

Costs and help

Scooters are not usually provided by the NHS. Some people use the Motability Scheme with the higher rate mobility part of certain benefits. Charities and second-hand options may help. Get any second-hand scooter serviced.

Staying active

Keep walking where you can, alongside using a scooter, to maintain strength.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Do I need a licence?

No, but Class 3 scooters must be registered.

Can the NHS provide a scooter?

Usually not, though wheelchair services may help with other needs.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: Care services, equipment and care homes
  • Age UK: Understanding frailty

If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111 (NHS 24 on 111 in Scotland; in Northern Ireland, your GP or GP out-of-hours service).
